Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

age noun

how old someone is; a time of life

also at that age, of that age, at my age, at your age, at his age, the same age, time of life, years old, at the age of fifteen, at age fifteen, in my twenty-first year, in his tenth year, over sixty, over sixty years old, more than … years old, less than … years old, period of life, in his fifteenth year, in my fourth year, under twenty years of age

classical

Quint. 1 pr. 6: cujus prīma aetās manifestum jam ingeniī lūmen ostendit
Traupman 269

aetās, aetātis f.

noun, third declension

age, time of life

Someone’s age and a stage of life: prīma aetās, early years. It is also a lifetime and an age of history (see life, generation).

Other words

  • id aetātis — at that age, of that age

    fixed phrase: the neuter id with a genitive, used like an adjective or adverb; so hoc aetātis, at this age · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 6.20.3: id aetātis jam sumus, we have now reached that time of life (Lewis & Short s.v. aetās); Cic. Att. 4.16.3: hominem id aetātis

    The phrase does not change with its noun: homō id aetātis, a man of that age; id aetātis sumus, we are of an age. So also id temporis, at that time.

  • … annōs nātus (nāta) — … years old

    participle agreeing with the person, with the accusative of the number of years · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 3.74: annōs nātus ūnum et vīgintī (Lewis & Short s.v. nāscor)

    The ordinary way to state an age. With a noun the genitive also serves: puer trium annōrum, a boy of three (see how old are you?, a man of).

  • … annum agēns — in one’s …th year: one year more than the years completed

    present participle of agō with an ordinal in the accusative · also used · classical · Suet. Caes. 1: annum agēns sextum decimum patrem āmīsit (Lewis & Short s.v. agō); Cic. Sen. 32: quārtum agō annum et octōgēsimum; Liv. 40.6.4: trīcēsimum annum agēns (Lewis & Short s.v. trīcēsimus); Traupman 76, 77

    Latin counts the year one is living through, so the ordinal is always one more than the age in years: a child who is three, trēs annōs nātus, quārtum annum agit, is in his fourth year, because the first year runs from birth to the first birthday. So decimum quīntum annum agēns is fourteen, not fifteen as Traupman renders it (“at age fifteen”); “at fifteen” is quīndecim annōs nātus. Lewis & Short itself renders Cicero’s quārtum annum agō et octōgēsimum loosely, “am eighty-four years old”.

  • mājor (minor) quam … annōs nātus — over (under) … years old

    comparative agreeing with the person; quam may be left out without changing the case · also used · classical · Cic. Rosc. Am. 39: annōs nātus mājor quadrāgintā, over forty years old (Lewis & Short s.v. magnus); Nep. Reg. 2.3: mājor annōs sexāgintā nātus dēcessit (Lewis & Short); Traupman 77

Examples

  • sī hominem id aetātis in tam longō sermōne diūtius retinuisset

    if he had kept a man of that age any longer in so long a conversationCic. Att. 4.16.3

  • quattuor et vīgintī fermē annōs nātus

    about twenty-four years oldLiv. 26.18.7

  • quārtum agō annum et octōgēsimum

    I am in my eighty-fourth yearCic. Sen. 32

  • Erat decem annōs nātus.

    He was ten years old.Traupman 77

  • Decem annōs est nātus. Ūndecimum agit (aetātis annum).

    He’s ten: he is in his eleventh year.Fōrm. VI 19

  • annum agēns sextum decimum patrem āmīsit

    in his sixteenth year (at fifteen) he lost his fatherSuet. Caes. 1 (Lewis & Short s.v. agō)

  • Minor vīgintī annōrum est.

    He is under twenty.Traupman 269
